Imagine pressing your finger into a piece of soft clay. Your finger leaves behind a small hollow, a pushed-in space, on the surface. That pushed-in space is an indentation.

An indentation is a space, gap, notch, or hollow that goes inward — into a surface, an edge, or a line of text. It is the result of something being pushed in, cut into, or set back from the surrounding area.

1. A Physical Hollow or Mark on a Surface

This is the most literal meaning. When a surface has a dent, a notch, a groove, or any kind of pushed-in mark, that mark is called an indentation.

Examples:

  • A car door that has been hit has an indentation on its surface.
  • A pillow after you sleep on it has an indentation in the shape of your head.
  • A bullet that hits a wall leaves an indentation in the plaster.
  • A key has many small indentations along its edge — those jagged cuts are what make each key unique.

The key idea here: the surface is not flat or smooth anymore. Something has gone inward, creating a hollow or dip.

2. A Jagged, Cut-In Shape Along an Edge

When the edge of something has cuts, notches, or irregular sections that go inward, those cut-in sections are called indentations. This meaning is very common when describing natural landscapes or the edges of objects.

Examples:

  • A coastline with many bays, coves, and inlets has many indentations — places where the sea cuts into the land.
  • The edge of a leaf often has small indentations that give it a jagged, tooth-like border.
  • The border between two countries drawn on a map may have several indentations where one country's land pushes into another's.

Think of it as: anywhere an edge bites inward rather than staying straight, that inward bite is an indentation.

3. The Blank Space at the Start of a Line of Text

This is a meaning you will encounter very often in reading, writing, and computing. When a line of text does not start at the leftmost edge of the page — when it is pushed a little to the right, leaving a blank gap at the beginning — that blank gap is called an indentation.

Examples:

  • In many books and essays, the first line of every new paragraph begins with a small blank space before the first word. That space is an indentation.
  • When you press the Tab key at the start of a line in a word processor, you create an indentation.
  • In computer programming, programmers use indentation — spaces or tabs at the start of lines — to visually show which lines of code belong together and which are nested inside others.

The purpose of this kind of indentation is organization and clarity. It signals to the reader: "Something new begins here," or "This part belongs inside that part."

All three meanings share the same underlying idea: something is set back, pushed in, or carved inward from the surrounding boundary.

  • On a surface → a dip or hollow pushed inward.
  • On an edge → a notch or cut that goes inward.
  • On a line of text → blank space pushed inward from the left margin.

In every case, there is a reference point (a flat surface, a straight edge, a left margin), and the indentation is the part that retreats from that reference point.

• An indentation → one specific hollow, notch, or text gap.
  • Indentations → multiple such hollows, notches, or gaps.

"The rock face was covered in small indentations where ancient fossils had been removed."

One Sentence to Remember It All

An indentation is any space, hollow, or gap that goes inward — whether it's a dent on a surface, a notch along an edge, or a blank space at the start of a line of text.

Once you see the concept of "going inward from a boundary," you will recognize the word indentation correctly in any context you ever encounter it.
